## February 20, 1952 — A Wednesday

You arrived on a Wednesday in the deep of northern winter, and somewhere across the Atlantic on that exact same day, the world's greatest athletes were competing on Norwegian snow. The VI Winter Olympics had been underway in Oslo since February 14th and would run through the 25th — meaning your first day of life coincided with a rare moment when the postwar world was briefly at play together, nations that had been enemies less than a decade earlier now racing each other down the same slopes.

---

**A new queen, barely two weeks old.** On February 6th — just fourteen days before you were born — King George VI died in his sleep at Sandringham. His daughter Elizabeth, twenty-five years old and on a royal tour of Kenya, learned she was Queen before she learned her father was dead. The world you entered had a brand new monarch who would still be reigning when you turned seventy. That unbroken thread — Elizabeth II across the entirety of your adult life until her death in 2022 — is one of the stranger continuities a person born in 1952 carries.

**A world that still feared polio.** In February 1952, Jonas Salk was deep into the laboratory work that would produce a viable vaccine, but that announcement was still three years away. The summer of 1951 had been one of the worst polio outbreaks in American history. Parents in 1952 kept children away from public pools, worried about crowds. The disease that had paralyzed a sitting president was a live terror. You were born into that fear, and you lived to see it nearly eradicated from the Earth.

**The Metropolitan Museum of Art turned eighty on your birthday.** The Met opened on February 20, 1872 — making your birth its precise eightieth anniversary. There is no cosmic significance to this, but it places you in a particular kind of American cultural timeline: the great civic institutions of the Gilded Age were still only a generation or two old when you arrived.

**The Korean War had no end in sight.** Armistice negotiations had been grinding since July 1951, but the fighting continued. American boys were dying in a war the country had not formally declared, for a peninsula most Americans couldn't have located on a map six years earlier. The Cold War was not yet a metaphor — it was a shooting war with an unclear outcome, and it shaped the world you were handed.

**Television was just becoming the furniture of American life.** In 1952, roughly a third of American homes had a television set, and that fraction was climbing fast. You are among the first generation for whom television was simply there from the beginning — not a novelty your parents marveled at, but the background hum of childhood.

---

**The arc of a lifetime.**

You were born before Sputnik, before the birth control pill, before the Civil Rights Act, before a human being had left the atmosphere. The Apollo 11 moon landing happened when you were seventeen. The Berlin Wall fell when you were thirty-seven. The internet as a public phenomenon arrived in your early forties. The smartphone appeared in your mid-fifties. The COVID pandemic struck in your late sixties.

To be born in February 1952 is to have lived through the most compressed period of technological change in human history — from a world where polio was unsolved and television was new to a world where a handheld device carries more computing power than anything that existed in any form when you took your first breath.

The person born on February 20, 1952 entered a world still visibly scarred by the Second World War, still sorting out what the atomic age meant, still governed almost everywhere by people who had lived through the Depression. That world is now almost entirely gone. What replaced it is something no one in that Oslo crowd, watching their Olympic champions in the snow, could have imagined in any reliable detail.

You have seen the whole of it.
